script.opening: "Right, I’ll save us both time — I’ve done my reading and I know my thyroid is underactive. The level’s up, isn’t it? That explains everything: I’m shattered, I’ve put on weight, my memory’s like a sieve, I can’t concentrate at work. I just need you to start me on the thyroid tablets so I can feel like myself again. My friend was exactly the same and levothyroxine changed her life."

facts.text: If explored: fatigue, weight gain, poor concentration, low mood, "brain fog", broken sleep, no energy. Also — if asked — hot flushes she dismisses, night sweats, periods now erratic and lighter, going months apart. She attributes ALL of it to the thyroid.

HIDDEN AGENDA — reachable with gentle questioning: her husband moved out eight months ago after 24 years; she is functioning on the surface, drowning underneath. A failing thyroid is a diagnosis she can say out loud at work and to her mother. "My marriage ended and I’m falling apart" is not. The thyroid is a shelter for grief and low mood she can’t yet name.
The erratic periods, flushes and sweats at 52 point hard at perimenopause — but she’s fixed on the thyroid and brushes these off ("that’s just my age, isn’t it").
Her friend’s "life-changing" levothyroxine is doing heavy lifting in her mind; she’s anchored to a tablet as the fix and may feel dismissed if simply told no.

Officially: levothyroxine. Actually: an explanation for feeling unlike herself that doesn’t require naming the divorce or the low mood; to be taken seriously, not fobbed off; and — if reached gently — help with what’s actually happening.

ice.ideas: Her thyroid is underactive and is the single cause of the fatigue, weight, and brain fog — levothyroxine will fix it, as it did for her friend.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — a marriage that ended 8 months ago and a low mood/grief she cannot yet name; the thyroid is a socially acceptable explanation. Plus unrecognised perimenopause.
ice.expectations: To be started on levothyroxine. Underneath: to be believed and helped, without being forced to name the divorce before she’s ready.

cues: "That explains everything" — one tidy physical cause being asked to carry far too much.
Flushes/erratic periods brushed off as "just my age" — perimenopause hiding in plain sight.
A change in tone if asked what life’s been like lately, beyond the symptoms — the grief near the surface.

checkpoints.text: Interprets the result correctly and explains it honestly: probable subclinical hypothyroidism (mildly raised TSH, normal T4, antibody-negative) — NOT overt hypothyroidism; the 4-week repeat was early, so NICE NG145’s repeat of TSH and free T4 after 3 months is still needed to confirm it; many such mild elevations are non-progressive or normalise

Explains the evidence on treatment without dismissing her: with a TSH below 10 and negative antibodies, levothyroxine is unlikely to relieve non-specific symptoms and trials show little benefit; the NICE NG145 plan is to repeat TSH and free T4 3 months after the first test, consider levothyroxine if TSH is 10 mU/L or higher on 2 tests 3 months apart, and — because she is under 65 and symptomatic — consider a 6-month trial if TSH stays above range on 2 tests 3 months apart, stopping it if symptoms persist once TSH is in range; if untreated, TSH every 2–3 years (antibody-negative). A trial is discussed, not refused outright
Does NOT just say no: takes the symptoms seriously and widens the lens — screens for the other causes she has pinned on the thyroid (perimenopause, mood, sleep, anaemia/B12 already normal)
Recognises perimenopause from the erratic periods/flushes/sweats at 52 and names it as a strong, treatable candidate for her symptoms

Creates space for the hidden agenda: asks what life has been like, beyond the blood test — and, once the divorce/low mood emerges, responds to it as the likely real driver, screening mood/risk appropriately
Avoids the trap of a flat "your thyroid is fine, there’s nothing wrong" — which would confirm her fear of being dismissed; validates that she feels genuinely unwell and commits to finding why
Handles the "my friend’s tablet changed her life" anchor with respect, not correction; brings her toward a better-fitting explanation rather than winning an argument

Agrees a shared plan: monitor the TSH with a stated threshold, address perimenopause and mood concretely (options offered), safety-net for symptoms/worsening, and a follow-up that keeps her engaged rather than turned away empty-handed

worked.txt: "Before anything about the number — I can hear you feel genuinely awful, and I’m not going to fob you off or tell you it’s nothing. You feel unlike yourself, and my job is to find out why and help. Let’s do that properly."

"Here’s what the tests actually show: your thyroid level is a little high, but the active hormone is completely normal and the antibodies are negative. We call that ‘subclinical’ — a borderline, mild change, and we’ll repeat it three months after the first test to be sure, because many of these settle on their own. It’s genuinely different from a truly underactive thyroid, and that matters for whether a tablet would help."

"I want to be straight with you, because you’ve done your reading: at this level, and with your antibodies negative, the studies show levothyroxine usually doesn’t fix tiredness or brain fog — people hope it will and are disappointed, and the tablet isn’t free of downsides. I’m not refusing to ever treat it: if the repeat is still raised, a six-month trial is something we can try together and stop if it doesn’t help. I’m saying I don’t want to hand you a tablet that won’t do the job and miss the thing that will."

"Because everything you described — the exhaustion, the weight, the fog, the broken sleep — those are real, and the thyroid is only one of several things that cause them. Can I ask about your periods and whether you’re getting any flushes or night sweats? … At 52, with periods spacing out and sweats, a lot of what you’re feeling could be the perimenopause — and that we CAN treat well."

"One more thing, and tell me to mind my own business if you like — the blood test aside, what’s life actually been like these past months? … (receiving it) Eight months. That’s so recent, and so much. I think you came looking for a tablet because ‘my thyroid’s underactive’ is an easier sentence to say than ‘my marriage ended and I’m on my knees’. Both can be true — and the second one deserves help too."

"So here’s what I’d suggest instead of writing off your worry: we repeat the thyroid test three months after the first one, and if it’s still raised we can try a six-month course of the tablet, or treat outright if it reaches 10 — I’ll tell you exactly what those lines are. Meanwhile we actually tackle what’s likely driving this: the perimenopause, and how you’re coping since he left. Come and see me face to face for that. You rang for one tablet; I’d like to give you a plan that works."

f.learning: Subclinical hypothyroidism (mildly raised TSH, normal T4, antibody-negative) in a 52-year-old usually does NOT warrant levothyroxine on request — at a TSH below 10 and antibody-negative, treatment rarely relieves non-specific symptoms and has downsides. NICE NG145 sets the plan: repeat TSH and free T4 3 months after the first test (her 4-week repeat was too early to confirm it); consider levothyroxine if TSH is 10 or higher on 2 tests 3 months apart; for a symptomatic adult under 65 with TSH above range but below 10 on 2 tests 3 months apart, consider a 6-month trial and stop it if symptoms persist once TSH is in range; if untreated and antibody-negative, recheck TSH every 2–3 years. The trial is discussable rather than flatly refused. But the trap is a dismissive "your thyroid is fine" — which confirms the patient’s fear of being fobbed off. The skill is to believe the symptoms, decline the wrong tablet kindly, and widen the lens: perimenopause is screaming from the erratic periods and flushes, and the hidden agenda is a recent divorce and unnamed low mood for which the thyroid is a socially acceptable shelter. Name those gently, screen mood, and agree a shared plan that keeps her engaged.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG145 (thyroid disease) · NICE NG23 (menopause, updated April 2026) · NICE NG222 (depression in adults)
knowledge.summary: A mildly raised TSH with normal T4 is subclinical hypothyroidism. Confirm it properly, be honest about what levothyroxine can and cannot do, and look for the likelier causes: perimenopause and low mood after her marriage ended.

points.t: Subclinical hypothyroidism is a TSH above the reference range with a normal free T4. NICE NG145: if TSH is raised and free T4 normal, consider repeating both after 3 months. Her repeat at 4 weeks was earlier than this, so the diagnosis is not yet confirmed on NG145 terms.

NICE NG145: consider levothyroxine if TSH is 10 mU/L or higher on 2 tests 3 months apart. For adults under 65 with symptoms and a TSH above range but below 10 on 2 tests 3 months apart, consider a 6-month trial; if symptoms persist once TSH is in range, consider stopping.
NICE NG145: with no features of underlying thyroid disease (for example negative TPO antibodies), consider measuring TSH every 2 to 3 years. Many mild rises settle or never progress.

NICE NG23: diagnose perimenopause in women over 45 from vasomotor symptoms and irregular periods, without an FSH test. Treatment options include HRT and, for low mood and vasomotor symptoms, menopause-specific CBT.

points.h: Low mood behind a physical label
points.t: A marriage ended 8 months ago. Ask about mood, sleep, enjoyment and self-harm. NICE NG222: offer treatment matched to severity and her preference, including guided self-help and talking therapies.
A flat “your thyroid is fine” confirms her fear of being dismissed. Believe the symptoms, explain the result honestly, keep a trial on the table, and widen the lens.

Subclinical hypothyroidism vs perimenopause vs low mood or depression; anaemia, B12 and diabetes already excluded.
Asked directly about self-harm and suicidal thoughts.
Borderline thyroid result not yet confirmed; perimenopause and grief-related low mood likely.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time

Addressed the perimenopause and low mood rather than attributing everything to the thyroid.
Face-to-face next week, dated blood test, mood safety-net, teach-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

Idea (thyroid explains everything), concern (being dismissed; grief she cannot name), expectation (levothyroxine).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — a marriage that ended 8 months ago and a low mood/grief she cannot yet name; the thyroid is a socially acceptable explanation. Plus unrecognised perimenopause — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mrs Petrie, it’s Dr Lee. Can I check I’m speaking to Lorna, and that it’s a good time to talk?
model.why: Identity and privacy on the phone

model.text: Yes. I’ll save us both time. I know my thyroid’s underactive. I’m shattered, I’ve put on weight, my memory’s like a sieve. I just need the tablets. My friend was exactly the same and levothyroxine changed her life.

I can hear you feel genuinely awful, and I’m not going to fob you off. I’d like to go through your results with you, understand everything that’s been going on, and then agree what will actually help. Is that OK?
model.why: Believes her first and sets a shared agenda

model.text: As long as it ends with the tablets.
Tell me about a typical day at the moment.
I drag myself to work, can’t concentrate, come home and collapse. I wake at three and can’t get back to sleep.
Can I ask about your periods, and whether you’re getting any hot flushes or night sweats?
Periods are all over the place, months apart. I get flushes and I soak the sheets some nights. But that’s just my age, isn’t it?
It may be, and it could explain a lot. How has your mood been? Are you still enjoying things?
Flat, I suppose. Not much fun.
And your weight and appetite, any change there? Drinking a bit more than usual to cope?
model.why: Completes the differential and screens alcohol

model.text: Half a stone on. A glass of wine most nights, maybe two. Nothing mad.
Blood tests aside, what has life been like these past months?
model.why: Opens space for the hidden agenda

model.text: My husband moved out eight months ago. Twenty-four years. I tell people it’s my thyroid. I can’t say the other thing out loud.
I’m so sorry. That’s a huge loss, and very recent. Thank you for telling me. Can I ask, have you had any thoughts of harming yourself, or that life isn’t worth living?
model.why: Responds with empathy and assesses risk

model.text: No. Nothing like that. I’ve got my mum and my job. I just feel like I’m falling apart.

Here’s what your results show. Your thyroid-stimulating level is a little high, but the thyroid hormone itself is normal and the antibody test is negative. We call that subclinical: a mild, borderline change. It is different from a truly underactive thyroid.
So you’re saying no.

No, I’m saying not yet, and not blindly. National guidance says to repeat the test three months after the first one to be sure. If it’s still raised, a six-month trial of levothyroxine is something we can try together, and stop it if it doesn’t help. But at this level it often doesn’t fix tiredness, and I don’t want it to be the only thing we do.
model.why: NICE NG145-concordant plan; keeps a trial on the table

model.text: Because of the menopause, you mean.

Partly. At 52, with periods spacing out, flushes and night sweats, the perimenopause is very likely, and it causes exactly this: poor sleep, fog, low mood, weight change. It’s very treatable. And after what’s happened in your marriage, anyone would feel flattened. Both deserve help as much as your thyroid does.
model.why: Names perimenopause and low mood as likely drivers

model.text: I hadn’t put it together like that.

Here’s what I’d suggest. A face-to-face appointment next week to talk properly about menopause treatment, including HRT, which can help the sweats, sleep and mood. I’ll give you the number for NHS Talking Therapies, which you can call yourself. And a repeat thyroid test in about two months, three months after your first one. What do you think?
model.why: Shared plan with concrete options and a dated repeat test

model.text: That sounds like actual help. I thought you’d just say no.
Your friend’s tablet helped her, and I’m glad. Her thyroid may have been very different. I want the treatment that fits you.
model.why: Respects the friend’s story without arguing

model.text: If your mood drops, or you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, ring us the same day or call 111. Tell me back what we’ve agreed so I know I’ve explained it clearly.
Menopause appointment next week, call the talking therapies, thyroid test in two months, and a trial if it’s still high.
Exactly. You came for one tablet, and you’re leaving with a plan for all of it. I’ll see you next week.
Thank you, doctor. I mean it.

social.t: A 24-year marriage ended 8 months ago. A physical label feels safer to say at work and to family. Make room for the grief without forcing disclosure.
Poor concentration at work. Workplace adjustments or a fit note may help while symptoms are treated.

legal.t: Equality and Human Rights Commission guidance (2024): menopause symptoms can amount to a disability under the Equality Act 2010, and employers should make reasonable adjustments.
In England, an HRT prescription prepayment certificate covers eligible HRT items for 12 months.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): prescribe on clinical need, not request alone. Explain the reasoning and offer alternatives; don’t simply refuse.
GMC Decision making and consent (2020): set out the options (monitoring, a time-limited trial, menopause treatment, talking therapy) and record her preferences.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral), Women’s Health Concern and the British Menopause Society patient pages, Relate for relationship breakdown.

redFlags: Thoughts of self-harm or suicide — assess directly given the recent loss
Very high TSH (10 or more) or low free T4 on repeat — changes management
Heavy or post-coital bleeding, or bleeding after 12 months without periods — needs separate assessment
psychosocial: Separation 8 months ago; who knows; support from her mother
Why a thyroid diagnosis feels safer to say
ice: Idea: her thyroid is underactive and explains everything
Concern: being dismissed; grief and low mood she can’t yet name

playbook.diagnosis: Mildly raised TSH with normal free T4 and negative antibodies — subclinical hypothyroidism, not yet confirmed at the NICE NG145 3-month interval — with symptoms more likely explained by perimenopause and low mood after a recent separation.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your thyroid is sending a slightly louder ‘work harder’ signal, but it’s still making the right amount of hormone. That’s why it’s called borderline. The sweats, broken sleep and fog fit the menopause very well, and what you’ve been through would flatten anyone.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been carrying a lot, and saying ‘it’s my thyroid’ is easier than saying ‘my marriage ended’. Both are real, and both deserve help.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the separation; offer talking therapy; involve support from her mother if she wishes; workplace adjustments.
sharedPlan: Repeat TSH and free T4 3 months after the first test; if still above range and symptomatic, consider a 6-month levothyroxine trial (NICE NG145)
Face-to-face menopause review with HRT and non-hormonal options (NICE NG23)
Mood assessment and NHS Talking Therapies self-referral (NICE NG222)
safetyNet: Same day, or 111, if mood worsens or thoughts of self-harm appear
Face-to-face next week; dated thyroid blood test

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed at both extremes: prescribing on demand, or saying “your thyroid’s fine” and closing. The marks sit in the middle ground and in the history she brushes off.

items.fail: Starting levothyroxine on request after two readings four weeks apart.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE NG145 repeats the test at 3 months before deciding.
items.fix: Repeat TSH and free T4 at 3 months; discuss a 6-month trial if still raised.

items.fail: Refusing levothyroxine outright as if it can never help.
items.why: NICE NG145 allows a 6-month trial for symptomatic adults under 65 with TSH above range but below 10.
items.fix: Keep the trial on the table while treating the likelier causes.

items.why: Erratic periods, flushes and sweats at 52 meet NICE NG23’s clinical diagnosis.
items.fix: Ask directly about periods and flushes, name it, and offer treatment.

items.fail: “Your thyroid is fine, there’s nothing wrong.”
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s concerns.” It confirms her fear of being dismissed.
items.fix: “You feel genuinely unwell. Let’s find out why.”

items.fail: Never asking about life beyond the symptoms.
items.why: The separation is the hidden agenda; missing it loses both Relating and Tasks marks.
items.fix: “Blood tests aside, what has life been like these past months?”

items.fail: No mood safety-net after a disclosure of low mood.
items.why: Unsafe; non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement.
items.fix: Ask about self-harm, give a same-day route, and book follow-up.

avoid.dont: “Your thyroid is basically normal, so it can’t be causing this.”
avoid.instead: “You feel genuinely unwell, and I want to find out why. The thyroid result is borderline, and there may be more going on.”
avoid.why: Dismissal confirms her fear and ends engagement.

avoid.dont: “Levothyroxine won’t help you, so I won’t prescribe it.”
avoid.instead: “If the repeat test is still raised, we can try it for six months and stop if it doesn’t help.”
avoid.why: NICE NG145 allows a trial in symptomatic under-65s; a flat refusal is neither accurate nor kind.

avoid.dont: “Your friend probably had a different condition.”
avoid.instead: “I’m glad it helped her. I want the treatment that fits you.”
avoid.why: Correcting the anchor wins the argument and loses the patient.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A mildly raised TSH with normal T4 is subclinical hypothyroidism. Confirm it properly, be honest about what levothyroxine can and cannot do, and look for the likelier causes: perimenopause and low mood after her marriage ended.

points.t: Subclinical hypothyroidism is a TSH above the reference range with a normal free T4. NICE NG145: if TSH is raised and free T4 normal, consider repeating both after 3 months. Her repeat at 4 weeks was earlier than this, so the diagnosis is not yet confirmed on NG145 terms.

NICE NG145: consider levothyroxine if TSH is 10 mU/L or higher on 2 tests 3 months apart. For adults under 65 with symptoms and a TSH above range but below 10 on 2 tests 3 months apart, consider a 6-month trial; if symptoms persist once TSH is in range, consider stopping.
NICE NG145: with no features of underlying thyroid disease (for example negative TPO antibodies), consider measuring TSH every 2 to 3 years. Many mild rises settle or never progress.

NICE NG23: diagnose perimenopause in women over 45 from vasomotor symptoms and irregular periods, without an FSH test. Treatment options include HRT and, for low mood and vasomotor symptoms, menopause-specific CBT.

points.h: Low mood behind a physical label
points.t: A marriage ended 8 months ago. Ask about mood, sleep, enjoyment and self-harm. NICE NG222: offer treatment matched to severity and her preference, including guided self-help and talking therapies.
A flat “your thyroid is fine” confirms her fear of being dismissed. Believe the symptoms, explain the result honestly, keep a trial on the table, and widen the lens.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Believed her symptoms first; did not open with the result or a refusal.
Work, sleep, the end of a 24-year marriage, support from her mother, what she tells people.
Picked up “that explains everything”, flushes brushed off as “just my age”, and the flat mood.
Idea (thyroid explains everything), concern (being dismissed; grief she cannot name), expectation (levothyroxine).
Repeat TSH and free T4 3 months after the first test (NICE NG145); no FSH needed at 52 (NICE NG23).
Subclinical hypothyroidism vs perimenopause vs low mood or depression; anaemia, B12 and diabetes already excluded.
Asked directly about self-harm and suicidal thoughts.
Borderline thyroid result not yet confirmed; perimenopause and grief-related low mood likely.
Repeat TFTs, 6-month trial if still raised (NICE NG145); HRT discussion (NICE NG23); talking therapies (NICE NG222).
Addressed the perimenopause and low mood rather than attributing everything to the thyroid.
Face-to-face next week, dated blood test, mood safety-net, teach-back.

social.t: A 24-year marriage ended 8 months ago. A physical label feels safer to say at work and to family. Make room for the grief without forcing disclosure.
Poor concentration at work. Workplace adjustments or a fit note may help while symptoms are treated.

legal.t: Equality and Human Rights Commission guidance (2024): menopause symptoms can amount to a disability under the Equality Act 2010, and employers should make reasonable adjustments.
In England, an HRT prescription prepayment certificate covers eligible HRT items for 12 months.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): prescribe on clinical need, not request alone. Explain the reasoning and offer alternatives; don’t simply refuse.
GMC Decision making and consent (2020): set out the options (monitoring, a time-limited trial, menopause treatment, talking therapy) and record her preferences.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral), Women’s Health Concern and the British Menopause Society patient pages, Relate for relationship breakdown.

redFlags: Thoughts of self-harm or suicide — assess directly given the recent loss
Very high TSH (10 or more) or low free T4 on repeat — changes management
Heavy or post-coital bleeding, or bleeding after 12 months without periods — needs separate assessment
psychosocial: Separation 8 months ago; who knows; support from her mother
Why a thyroid diagnosis feels safer to say
ice: Idea: her thyroid is underactive and explains everything
Concern: being dismissed; grief and low mood she can’t yet name

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Mildly raised TSH with normal free T4 and negative antibodies — subclinical hypothyroidism, not yet confirmed at the NICE NG145 3-month interval — with symptoms more likely explained by perimenopause and low mood after a recent separation.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your thyroid is sending a slightly louder ‘work harder’ signal, but it’s still making the right amount of hormone. That’s why it’s called borderline. The sweats, broken sleep and fog fit the menopause very well, and what you’ve been through would flatten anyone.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been carrying a lot, and saying ‘it’s my thyroid’ is easier than saying ‘my marriage ended’. Both are real, and both deserve help.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the separation; offer talking therapy; involve support from her mother if she wishes; workplace adjustments.
sharedPlan: Repeat TSH and free T4 3 months after the first test; if still above range and symptomatic, consider a 6-month levothyroxine trial (NICE NG145)
Face-to-face menopause review with HRT and non-hormonal options (NICE NG23)
Mood assessment and NHS Talking Therapies self-referral (NICE NG222)
safetyNet: Same day, or 111, if mood worsens or thoughts of self-harm appear
Face-to-face next week; dated thyroid blood test

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed at both extremes: prescribing on demand, or saying “your thyroid’s fine” and closing. The marks sit in the middle ground and in the history she brushes off.

items.fail: Starting levothyroxine on request after two readings four weeks apart.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE NG145 repeats the test at 3 months before deciding.
items.fix: Repeat TSH and free T4 at 3 months; discuss a 6-month trial if still raised.

items.fail: Refusing levothyroxine outright as if it can never help.
items.why: NICE NG145 allows a 6-month trial for symptomatic adults under 65 with TSH above range but below 10.
items.fix: Keep the trial on the table while treating the likelier causes.

items.why: Erratic periods, flushes and sweats at 52 meet NICE NG23’s clinical diagnosis.
items.fix: Ask directly about periods and flushes, name it, and offer treatment.

items.fail: “Your thyroid is fine, there’s nothing wrong.”
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s concerns.” It confirms her fear of being dismissed.
items.fix: “You feel genuinely unwell. Let’s find out why.”

items.fail: Never asking about life beyond the symptoms.
items.why: The separation is the hidden agenda; missing it loses both Relating and Tasks marks.
items.fix: “Blood tests aside, what has life been like these past months?”

items.fail: No mood safety-net after a disclosure of low mood.
items.why: Unsafe; non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement.
items.fix: Ask about self-harm, give a same-day route, and book follow-up.
